title: Given a `List<Employee>`, sort them by their year of joining so that the most recently joined employees appear first (descending year).
shortTitle: Sort employees by year of joining (most recent first)

s1_definition.profdef: Sorting most-recent-first is a single-key descending sort on an `int` year. You can express it as `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getYearOfJoining).reversed()`, or as `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getYearOfJoining, Comparator.reverseOrder())`-style via a boxed key. The `reversed()` call flips the ascending natural order into descending.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants a "newest joiners first" list for its onboarding review — the people who joined most recently should be at the top. So we order by joining year, but flipped: the biggest year (latest) comes first.
s1_definition.oneliner: `comparingInt(year).reversed()` puts the latest-joining employees at the top.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sorting most-recent-first is a single-key descending sort on an `int` year. You can express it as `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getYearOfJoining).reversed()`, or as `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getYearOfJoining, Comparator.reverseOrder())`-style via a boxed key. The `reversed()` call flips the ascending natural order into descending.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants a "newest joiners first" list for its onboarding review — the people who joined most recently should be at the top. So we order by joining year, but flipped: the biggest year (latest) comes first.

**One line to remember:** `comparingInt(year).reversed()` puts the latest-joining employees at the top.

sections.s2_technical:
`Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getYearOfJoining)` orders ascending — oldest year first. Calling `.reversed()` on that comparator returns a new comparator with the opposite verdict, so the largest year (the most recent) sorts first. For example, an employee who joined in 2022 will now come before one who joined in 2015.

An important detail: `comparingInt` returns a specialised comparator and `.reversed()` works cleanly on it. If you had used `comparing(Employee::getYearOfJoining)` with a boxed Integer, `.reversed()` still works but you pay the boxing cost. Either way the source list is untouched because `sorted` creates a new stream.

If two employees joined in the same year and you want a deterministic tie-break, you append `thenComparing(Employee::getName)` after the reversed year comparator. Note the ordering of calls: reverse the year first, then add the tie-breaker, so the tie-breaker is not accidentally reversed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a 90-day onboarding review and wants the most recently joined staff at the top of the list so the onboarding team acts on them first. A normal ascending sort would bury the newest joiners at the bottom. This is exactly how a reversed year comparator works — it floats the latest joiners to the top.

Problem 2 — Several people joined the same year, and the review list must be stable. This is exactly how an appended name tie-breaker works — same-year employees are ordered alphabetically.

The code defines `Employee`, an `OnboardingService` with `sortByJoiningDesc`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh 2015, Priya 2022, Amit 2022, Sneha 2019, Vikram 2010.

Step 1: The base comparator orders by year ascending (2010, 2015, 2019, 2022, 2022).

Step 2: `.reversed()` flips the verdict, so the largest year wins — the two 2022 joiners come first, then 2019, 2015, 2010.

Step 3: The appended name tie-breaker orders the two 2022 joiners: Amit before Priya.

Step 4: `toList()` returns a new list; input untouched.

```
INFO: Onboarding review (newest joiners first):
INFO:   joined 2022 | Amit
INFO:   joined 2022 | Priya
INFO:   joined 2019 | Sneha
INFO:   joined 2015 | Rajesh
INFO:   joined 2010 | Vikram
```

```
  Input: [Rajesh/2015, Priya/2022, Amit/2022, Sneha/2019, Vikram/2010]
    │
    ▼
  sorted( comparingInt(year).reversed().thenComparing(name) )
    │
    ├─ base: year asc  → 2010,2015,2019,2022,2022
    ├─ reversed() → 2022,2022,2019,2015,2010
    └─ tie 2022 → name A→Z → Amit, Priya
    ▼
  toList() → NEW list
    ▼
  Output: Amit/2022, Priya/2022, Sneha/2019, Rajesh/2015, Vikram/2010
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To sort employees most-recent-first I use a single descending key on the year of joining. I build `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getYearOfJoining)` which is ascending by default, and then call `.reversed()` to flip it so the largest year, meaning the latest joiner, comes first.

The one subtlety I always point out is call ordering. I reverse the year comparator first and only then append a name tie-breaker with `thenComparing`, so that the tie-breaker is applied in normal ascending order and is not accidentally reversed along with the year. If I had written the chain the other way around the tie-break direction would have been wrong.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this produced the onboarding review list, floating the newest joiners to the top so the onboarding team worked the most urgent 90-day reviews first, with same-year joiners ordered alphabetically for a stable, reproducible roster. And like every stream sort, it returned a new list and left the source untouched.

---

keyPoints: reversed() for descending, thenComparing() for secondary sort
sorted() is stateful — buffers all elements before passing downstream
